title: Madagascar’s Giant Bats Are Getting Smaller
paragraphs: Researchers at the Field Museum in Chicago report that Madagascar’s flying foxes, among the largest bats in the world, have become smaller over the past few decades. The study, published in the Journal of Mammalogy, started when a scientist noticed that bats in museum collections looked bigger than the animals caught in the field today.

To test this idea, the team measured skulls and teeth of 121 specimens kept in nine museums. Skulls collected before the 1980s were about 3.6 millimetres, or 6 percent, longer than those collected after that time. The drop in size matches the period when hunting changed from small family hunts to a commercial trade, with bats sold at markets and restaurants. The researchers say hunters may prefer the biggest bats because they give the most meat. The population is also thought to have fallen from about 300,000 in the early 2000s by around two-thirds.

However, the study cannot prove that hunting is the cause. It is based on the timing of two changes, and other factors, such as habitat loss and climate change, could also play a role. More research, including genetic studies, is needed to show how healthy the bats are today.

questions.a: The skulls and teeth of 121 museum specimens.

questions.q: When did bats start to get smaller?
questions.a: Around the 1980s, when hunting became commercial.

questions.q: Why can the study not prove that hunting is the cause?
questions.a: It only shows a link in timing; habitat loss and climate change could also matter.
